glosses: to sharpen, to whet (to make sharp)
to tighten, to toughen (to make something stricter or more stringent)
to exacerbate (to cause a rapid deterioration in relations or the situation)
to sharpen (to make the shapes or outlines of something more clearly defined, e.g. facial features)
to sensitize (to cause someone to react strongly to sensory stimuli)
to spice up (to enhance the flavour of something using spice)
to sharpen up (to get more clearly outlined)
to tighten up, to toughen up (to become stricter or more stringent)
to exacerbate (to take a violent form)
to get sensitized (to start reacting strongly to sensory stimuli)
w stosunku do przepisów, reguł, sankcji: czynić mniej liberalnymi, bardziej ograniczającymi lub grożącymi wyższymi karami
w stosunku do sytuacji, konfliktu, polemiki: wzmacniać ich intensywność

examples.text: to sharpen a pencil or a knife or a musical note
He that wrestles with us strengthens our nerves and sharpens our skill.

The use of algorithms in policing is one example of their increasing influence on our lives.[…]who, if anyone, is policing their use. Such concerns were sharpened further by the continuing revelations about how the US National Security Agency (NSA) has been using algorithms to help it interpret the colossal amounts of data it has collected from its covert dragnet of international telecommunications.

The organizers said they had found themselves "more involved in the web of social convulsions and violence that is tormenting our country. The present economic crisis, the grave political instability and the rapidly sharpening violence have finally overtaken […] our wishes.

glosses: To hone or rub on with some substance, as a piece of stone, for the purpose of sharpening – see whetstone.

examples.text: And the Mower whets his ſithe,
Why dost thou whet thy knife so earnestly?
Here roams the wolf, the eagle whets his beak.

glosses: To stimulate or make more keen.

examples.text: to whet one's appetite or one's courage
Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar, / I have not slept.
My faith in vegetarianism grew on me from day to day. Salt's book whetted my appetite for dietetic studies. I went in for all books available on vegetarianism and read them.
In the end, porn doesn’t whet men’s appetites—it turns them off the real thing.

glosses: That which whets or sharpens; especially, an appetizer.

examples.text: sips, drams, and whets
To make a nice Whet before Dinner […]
A really good game, to my mind, must have an element, however slight, of physical danger to the player. This is the great whet to skilled performance.
Please tighten that screw a quarter-turn.
Just where I please, with tighten;d rein / I'll urge thee round the dusty plain.
That joint is tightening as the wood dries.

glosses: To make money harder to borrow or obtain.

examples.text: If the government doesn't tighten the money supply, inflation is certain to be harsh.
The Fed is expected to tighten by a quarter-point.

glosses: To make (an offence) worse or more severe; to increase in offensiveness or heinousness.

examples.text:
Once more, the more to aggrauate the note,
With a foule Traitors name ſtuffe I thy throte,
And wiſh (ſo pleaſe my Soueraigne) ere I moue,
What my tong ſpeaks, my right drawn ſword may proue
The defense made by the prisoner's counsel did rather aggravate than extenuate his crime.
to aggravate my woes.
[…] to aggravate the horrors of the scene

glosses: To give extra weight or intensity to; to exaggerate, to magnify.

examples.text: He aggravated the story.

glosses: To pile or heap (something heavy or onerous) on or upon someone.

examples.text: In order to lighten the crown still further, they aggravated responsibility on ministers of state.

glosses: To exasperate; to provoke or irritate.

examples.text: If both were to aggravate her parents, as my brother and sister do mine.
Ben Bella was aggravated by having to express himself in French because the Egyptians were unable to understand his Arabic.

glosses: o sytuacji, konflikcie, polemice: wzmacniać intensywność, eskalować

examples.text: to intensify the heat or cold
to intensify colors
to intensify a photographic negative
to intensify animosity

glosses: To become intense, or more intense; to act with increasing power or energy.

examples.text: Feminist critiques of continuity discourse have become increasingly audible within the mainstream Jewish world, intensifying last year after [Steven M.] Cohen himself was accused of serial sexual harassment.
